paragraphs: Reward models learn from human comparisons of model responses, making the choice of which responses to compare important when annotation is expensive. This paper studies how to select useful comparisons adaptively. Its central idea is that a good labeling dataset should cover different parts of the model’s representation space while including pairs whose rewards differ moderately.

The authors turn these goals into selection strategies using Fisher information, a statistical measure of how informative observations are about model parameters. They adapt ideas from classical experimental design to the final linear layer of a neural reward model. This provides a concrete way to prioritize comparisons while keeping the selection process computationally manageable.

Across multiple open-source language models and datasets, the method shows strong performance, efficiency, and stability relative to the selection methods evaluated. Additional experiments find that comparing responses across different prompts substantially improves labeling efficiency. Together, these results suggest that both coverage and the structure of comparisons matter when spending a limited human annotation budget.
icml-2025-active-reward-modeling-adaptiv.tldr: Fisher information guides the selection of human preference comparisons, improving reward-model labeling efficiency in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions as information arrives, so predictions can help them anticipate what comes next. The difficulty is deciding how much to trust that advice. This paper proposes using calibration to connect a predictor’s uncertainty estimates with the decisions an algorithm makes, instead of asking users to specify one overall level of trust.

The authors investigate this approach through ski rental and online job scheduling. For ski rental, they design an algorithm with nearly optimal performance that depends on the predictions it receives. They also prove that calibrated advice provides more effective guidance than the uncertainty alternatives considered when the setting has high variance. That qualification is part of the theoretical result.

For job scheduling, incorporating a calibrated predictor produces substantial improvements over existing methods. Evaluations using real-world data support the theoretical findings. The broader contribution is a way to make prediction uncertainty operational: confidence attached to individual predictions can guide online decisions more precisely than a single aggregate assessment of reliability.
icml-2025-algorithms-with-calibrated-mac.tldr: Calibrated prediction uncertainty improves online decision-making in ski rental and job scheduling.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks poison training data to implant hidden vulnerabilities in a neural network. Defenses that train a benign model from such data often depend on an additional trusted collection of clean examples. This paper addresses the setting where no such clean seed is available, and where elaborate feature analysis can make existing defenses costly.

Bi-perspective Splitting Defense, or BSD, identifies clean examples through two complementary views. One component uses semantic characteristics through open set recognition-based splitting. The other uses loss statistics through altruistic model-based splitting. The motivating observation is that defenders should make better use of accessible target labels and clean examples that are difficult for the model.

Experiments on benchmark datasets against representative attacks report an improvement of over 20% in average Defense Effectiveness Rating relative to existing defenses. The result supports combining semantic and loss-based evidence when separating usable training examples from poisoned data. Here, clean-seed-free defense means avoiding an additional trusted subset while still identifying clean samples within the available training collection.
icml-2025-bi-perspective-splitting-defen.tldr: BSD combines semantic and loss statistics to defend against backdoors without an additional trusted clean dataset.

paragraphs: Reassembling broken objects requires a robot to connect shape understanding with coordinated physical action. A fragment’s geometry matters for grasping it, aligning it with another piece, and moving both hands together. BiAssemble studies this geometric assembly problem, including action sequences that extend beyond a single grasp or placement.

The approach learns point-level affordances: information about which actions particular locations on an object support. It makes these affordances aware of collaboration between the robot’s two hands. This connects local geometric cues with the demands of a longer assembly sequence, using the ability of point-level affordances to generalize across different shapes.

The authors also introduce a real-world benchmark designed to combine varied fragment geometry with reproducible evaluation. This matters because differences between broken parts can otherwise make assembly results difficult to compare. Extensive experiments show the proposed approach outperforming the evaluated affordance-based and imitation-based methods. The findings support learning action possibilities that account for two-hand coordination when assembling geometrically diverse fragments.
icml-2025-biassemble-learning-collaborat.tldr: BiAssemble learns point-level action possibilities that help two robot hands coordinate the reassembly of broken objects.

paragraphs: Designing a molecule involves both discrete construction choices and continuous geometry. This paper introduces Compositional Generative Flows, or CGFlow, to handle objects built in stages while also modeling their continuous features. In its drug-design application, the system jointly proposes a synthetic pathway and the molecule’s three-dimensional binding pose.

The key technical idea extends the interpolation process used in flow matching to transitions between compositional states. The framework also draws on generative flow networks to guide sampling with rewards. These ingredients connect stepwise construction with continuous modeling, allowing synthesis decisions and spatial arrangement to be considered within one generative approach.

On all 15 LIT-PCBA targets, the authors report state-of-the-art binding affinity and synthesizability, together with 4.2 times better sampling efficiency than a two-dimensional synthesis-based baseline. They also report strong results on CrossDocked2020 for both Vina Dock and AiZynth success rate. These benchmark findings support joint optimization of molecular geometry and synthetic construction, rather than treating the generation of a molecule and its pathway as unrelated objectives.
icml-2025-compositional-flows-for-3d-mol.tldr: CGFlow jointly generates molecular synthesis pathways and three-dimensional binding poses through reward-guided compositional flow modeling.

paragraphs: Confounders influence both model inputs and prediction targets, creating correlations that can bias predictions. Their effects become especially troublesome in continual learning, where new data arrive over time and the model must retain earlier knowledge. If the relationships involving confounders change, a representation that worked earlier may become misleading later.

The paper introduces Recursive Metadata Normalization, or R-MDN, as a layer for removing confounder influence from intermediate features. It uses recursive least squares to maintain and update an internal statistical regression model as data and confounder distributions change. The layer is designed for insertion at any stage of a deep learning architecture, including vision transformers.

Experiments show more equitable predictions across population groups in both static learning and successive stages of continual learning. They also show reduced catastrophic forgetting associated with changing confounder effects. The contribution is an updating feature-normalization mechanism: it responds to evolving statistical relationships instead of relying on a single fixed adjustment, helping preserve useful representations as the learning setting changes.
icml-2025-confounder-free-continual-lear.tldr: R-MDN continually updates feature normalization to reduce changing confounder effects, improving group equity and reducing forgetting in experiments.

paragraphs: Visual autoregressive models often convert continuous visual information into discrete codes before generating it sequentially. That quantization can discard information. This paper develops a continuous framework that allows autoregressive visual generation without vector quantization, addressing the training objective needed when predictions remain in a continuous space.

Its foundation is strictly proper scoring rules, statistical tools for assessing how closely a predicted distribution matches the true distribution. Within the framework, choosing such a scoring rule supplies the objective to optimize during training. The authors focus primarily on energy-score objectives, which do not require likelihood evaluation and therefore address a difficulty of probabilistic prediction over continuous visual representations.

The framework also brings earlier continuous autoregressive approaches into a shared formulation. GIVT and diffusion loss can be derived through other choices of strictly proper scores. The contribution is therefore both a route to direct continuous generation and an explanation of how several existing methods relate. The scoring-rule perspective makes the choice of distributional training objective central to the design.
icml-2025-continuous-visual-autoregressi.tldr: Strictly proper scoring rules provide a unified framework for autoregressive visual generation without vector quantization.

paragraphs: Computational pathology often uses multiple instance learning to combine embeddings from enormous tissue images into patient-level representations. Training these models is difficult when clinical datasets are small and supervision is weak. This paper investigates whether pretrained multiple instance learning models can provide a useful starting point for new prediction tasks.

The study evaluates 11 models across 19 pretraining tasks covering tissue subtyping, cancer grading, and molecular subtype prediction. Fine-tuning pretrained models substantially improves performance over starting from random weights, including when the pretraining and target domains differ. Pretraining across multiple cancers also produces more consistent generalization across organs and task types than pretraining on a single disease.

In the reported comparison, this pan-cancer pretraining transfers better than a state-of-the-art slide-level foundation model while using only 6.5% as much training data. These findings support the adaptability of multiple instance learning architectures. They also indicate that the breadth of pretraining tasks and diseases can matter when building reusable models for pathology settings with limited labeled data.
icml-2025-do-multiple-instance-learning-.tldr: Pretrained multiple instance learning models transfer well across pathology tasks, with pan-cancer pretraining providing especially consistent benefits.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can memorize their training images, particularly when data are scarce. Attempts to reduce memorization have often come with worse image quality. This paper asks whether strong visual generation and low memorization can coexist, and uses the noise levels involved in diffusion training to examine where the tension arises.

The authors provide theoretical evidence that memorization is necessary only for denoising problems at low noise levels, which are commonly associated with generating fine visual details. This is a restriction on where necessity arises, rather than a claim that every low-noise problem must produce the same behavior. Motivated by the analysis, they propose training with noisy data at large noise scales.

The reported experiments show substantially reduced memorization without a decrease in image quality. This holds for both text-conditioned and unconditional models across several data-availability settings. The findings improve the observed trade-off between fidelity and memorization and suggest that changing how training uses noisy observations can preserve generation quality while reducing reliance on particular training examples.
icml-2025-does-generation-require-memori.tldr: Training diffusion models with noisy data at large noise scales reduces memorization without lowering image quality in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Transformer attention can concentrate too heavily on a small number of tokens, limiting how information moves through the model. Doubly stochastic attention imposes balance across both rows and columns of the attention matrix. Existing ways to enforce this structure commonly use repeated Sinkhorn normalization, introducing computational cost.

ESPFormer constructs doubly stochastic attention using Expected Sliced Transport Plans, drawing on sliced optimal transport. Its mechanism is fully parallelizable and avoids the iterative normalization required by the earlier approaches described in the paper. A temperature-based soft sorting operation makes the construction differentiable, so the attention mechanism can be trained within a deep neural network.

Experiments cover image classification, point cloud classification, sentiment analysis, and neural machine translation. Across these benchmarks, the authors report consistent performance improvements from the proposed attention regularization, alongside improved efficiency of enforcing the constraint. The work matters because it offers a different computational route to balanced attention, making that structural property available without the same iterative normalization procedure.
icml-2025-espformer-doubly-stochastic-at.tldr: ESPFormer uses parallelizable transport plans to enforce balanced attention without iterative Sinkhorn normalization.

paragraphs: Computer vision models still struggle to generalize to new tasks from instructions alone. This paper investigates whether conventional task names, such as image segmentation, provide too little explanation of what a model should do. The authors hypothesize that these compact labels hinder understanding of familiar tasks and consequently make unfamiliar tasks harder to interpret.

They replace such definitions with Explanatory Instructions: detailed language describing the transformation from an input image to the desired output. To train this behavior, they build a dataset containing 12 million image, instruction, and output triplets. An autoregressive vision-language model learns to produce outputs from both the image and the explanatory text.

The resulting model handles new instructions for previously encountered tasks and shows strong zero-shot generalization to unseen vision tasks. These are distinct forms of generalization: interpreting fresh descriptions of familiar objectives and following descriptions of new objectives. The findings support the proposed role of explanatory task language, while the claim that terminology is a key barrier remains the hypothesis motivating the study.
icml-2025-explanatory-instructions-towar.tldr: Detailed descriptions of image-to-output transformations help a vision-language model generalize to new instructions and unseen vision tasks.

paragraphs: Remote-sensing images pose challenges that ordinary photographs do not: overhead views, large changes in scale, and small objects within high-resolution scenes. Multimodal models also lack enough detailed, domain-specific examples connecting conversation to image regions. GeoPixel addresses these issues by linking conversational outputs to precise pixel masks in remote-sensing imagery.

The model supports images up to 4K resolution with arbitrary aspect ratios and can interleave segmentation masks with conversation. This gives its responses an explicit visual reference at the pixel level. The authors also construct GeoPixelD, a grounded conversation dataset, using a semi-automated process that combines set-of-marks prompting with spatial information tailored to remote sensing.

GeoPixel outperforms the existing multimodal models evaluated on segmentation involving both single and multiple targets. Component-removal studies also support the usefulness of the architecture’s individual parts. The contribution combines a model capable of detailed visual grounding with training data built for the same setting, addressing both the representation and data challenges behind remote-sensing conversation.
icml-2025-geopixel-pixel-grounding-large.tldr: GeoPixel combines high-resolution remote-sensing conversation with pixel masks and a domain-specific grounded dataset.

paragraphs: Generating a convincing talking face over a long video requires more than plausible individual frames. Head movement, facial expression, lip synchronization, and identity must remain coherent across time. This paper introduces the Motion-priors Conditional Diffusion Model, or MCDM, to use information from both earlier footage and the current clip when predicting motion.

An archived-clip component combines historical frames with a reference frame to preserve identity and context. A present-clip diffusion component models multimodal causal relationships for predicting head movement, expressions, and lip synchronization. A memory-efficient temporal attention mechanism stores and updates motion features dynamically, helping reduce errors that accumulate over an extended generation.

The authors also introduce TalkingFace-Wild, a multilingual dataset containing more than 200 hours of footage across 10 languages. Experiments demonstrate that MCDM maintains identity and motion continuity in long-term talking-face generation. The approach matters because it makes continuity an explicit part of motion prediction, combining the immediate clip’s requirements with a maintained representation of preceding motion.
icml-2025-long-term-talkingface-generati.tldr: MCDM combines historical and current motion information to preserve identity and movement continuity in long talking-face videos.

paragraphs: Extending a language model’s context window is useful only if it can effectively use the longer input while retaining its earlier capabilities. LongRoPE2 addresses both goals through changes to rotary positional embeddings, or RoPE. It begins with the hypothesis that insufficient training in higher RoPE dimensions contributes to problems when existing extension methods encounter unfamiliar sequence lengths.

The method uses evolutionary search to find RoPE rescaling choices, guided by a needle-driven perplexity measure. It then fine-tunes with mixed context windows: long sequences use the rescaled RoPE, while shorter sequences retain the original RoPE. This training arrangement supports adaptation to long inputs while preserving behavior within the original window.

Experiments on LLaMA3-8B and Phi3-mini-3.8B support the hypothesis and the method’s effectiveness. For LLaMA3-8B, the authors report an effective 128K context while retaining over 98.5% of short-context performance, using 10 billion training tokens. The stated comparison uses 80 times fewer tokens than Meta’s approach, which did not reach the target effective context length.
icml-2025-longrope2-near-lossless-llm-co.tldr: LongRoPE2 combines searched positional rescaling with mixed-window training to extend context while largely preserving short-context performance.

paragraphs: Long videos can produce more visual tokens than a language model’s context window can accommodate. LongVU addresses this by compressing video representations across both time and space while preserving useful visual detail. Its central idea is to use the text query and relationships between frames to identify information that can be reduced.

The process first uses DINOv2 features to remove frames that are highly similar to others. It then applies a text-guided cross-modal query to selectively reduce frame features. A further stage reduces spatial tokens across frames according to their temporal dependencies. These steps target different sources of redundancy within the same limited context budget.

The reported results show that LongVU processes many frames with little visual information loss and consistently outperforms existing methods across the evaluated video-understanding benchmarks. Gains are especially strong on hour-long video tasks in VideoMME and MLVU. The method also works effectively with a lightweight language model, supporting smaller systems while retaining strong video-understanding performance.
icml-2025-longvu-spatiotemporal-adaptive.tldr: LongVU compresses redundant video information using text queries and frame relationships to improve long-video understanding within limited context.

paragraphs: Learning rates control the size of parameter updates and strongly affect how efficiently a model trains. Choosing them through repeated hyperparameter searches can be expensive. MetaOptimize instead adjusts these training controls during the training run itself, with particular emphasis on step sizes.

The framework can wrap around any first-order optimization algorithm. Its objective is a specific form of regret that accounts for the longer-term effects of learning-rate choices through a discounted sum of future losses. This makes the consequences for subsequent training part of the tuning criterion, giving the method a way to assess step sizes beyond their immediate effect.

The authors also introduce variants with lower computational complexity. Across diverse machine learning tasks, these variants, together with the framework’s compatibility with different optimizers, achieve performance comparable to the best handcrafted learning-rate schedules considered. The contribution is an adaptive mechanism for tuning the training process, reducing reliance on an externally selected schedule while explicitly considering how current choices influence later losses.
icml-2025-metaoptimize-a-framework-for-o.tldr: MetaOptimize adjusts learning rates during training using an objective that accounts for their longer-term effects on loss.

paragraphs: Reconstructing fluid flow requires preserving small structures and changes across both space and time. Existing implicit neural representations can struggle with these details, and their assumption of grid independence can complicate use in simulation settings. This paper addresses the modeling problem alongside the shortage of standardized evaluation data.

The authors introduce HFR-Beach, a public 5.4-terabyte computational fluid dynamics dataset containing 33,600 unsteady two- and three-dimensional vector fields. Their PEINR model aims to improve numerical precision and grid resolution together. Its physical encoding separates temporal and spatial components, using Gaussian coordinate encoding and localized encoding to represent nonlinear dynamics and the spatial stencil structure.

A transformer-based spatiotemporal component then combines spatial and temporal information to capture dependencies over longer time spans. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations show better reconstruction quality than the state-of-the-art implicit representation methods compared. The contribution connects coordinate-based representation with simulation-relevant spatial structure and temporal information, while providing a large dataset for studying high-fidelity flow reconstruction.
icml-2025-peinr-a-physics-enhanced-impli.tldr: PEINR combines physical encoding and temporal attention to improve flow reconstruction, alongside a large public simulation dataset.

paragraphs: Vision-language models make publicly shared images easier to interpret automatically, creating a privacy challenge. Privacy-Shielded Image Compression, or PSIC, places a defense within the compression process. It produces a compressed bitstream with multiple decoding options, retaining ordinary compression functionality while controlling which reconstructed version is produced.

By default, decoding aims to preserve satisfactory perceptual quality while preventing interpretation by vision-language models. A customizable input condition enables reconstruction that preserves the image’s full semantic information. A conditional latent trigger module supplies information that steers the decoder toward different versions, making the decoding condition part of how image content is exposed.

Training uses an uncertainty-aware objective informed by soft labels from the target vision-language model. An adaptive multi-objective strategy jointly balances protection and perceptual quality. The authors report effectiveness across multiple downstream tasks and describe integration with most existing learned image compression models. The contribution is a flexible compression-and-decoding design whose reported protection is demonstrated through those model-based evaluations.
icml-2025-privacy-shielded-image-compres.tldr: PSIC adds condition-dependent decoding to image compression to preserve visual quality while obstructing vision-language model interpretation.

paragraphs: Dynamic treatment regimes personalize decisions as a patient’s condition changes, but learning recommendations is difficult when the optimal treatment is unknown. Existing approaches often treat clinician-prescribed treatments as definitive labels and primarily use structured records. SAFER combines structured electronic health records with clinical notes while explicitly addressing uncertainty in treatment labels.

Its tabular-language framework allows the two information sources to learn from each other. For patients who died, it assumes the optimal treatment solution is ambiguous rather than treating the observed treatment as an unambiguous target. It also uses conformal prediction to provide statistical guarantees and filter uncertain recommendations, incorporating risk awareness into the recommendation process.

On two public sepsis datasets, SAFER outperforms the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines across multiple recommendation metrics and counterfactual mortality rate. These findings concern recommendations evaluated on those datasets, including a counterfactual outcome measure. They support the potential of combining clinical text, structured data, and calibrated uncertainty for treatment recommendation, with the formal assurances belonging to the framework’s statistical prediction procedure.
icml-2025-safer-a-calibrated-risk-aware-.tldr: SAFER combines clinical notes, structured records, ambiguous treatment labels, and conformal prediction for risk-aware treatment recommendations.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more output tokens can allow more reasoning, but the training method affects how effectively it uses that budget. This paper compares learning by copying successful reasoning traces with methods that use verification to guide reinforcement learning or search. Its theoretical analysis establishes an advantage for verifier-based methods under a fixed compute or data budget.

The stronger scaling result depends on properties of the pretrained model. Correct solutions must be heterogeneous, such as differing in length or style, and the rewards of sampled traces must have a sufficiently spread-out distribution. The authors formalize this latter property through anti-concentration. Under these conditions, the gap favoring verifier-based approaches widens as the test-time token budget grows.

Experiments on didactic problems and mathematical reasoning with pretrained models of 3, 8, and 32 billion parameters support the theory. The findings explain why additional generation alone may yield disappointing scaling when training only imitates successful traces. Verification supplies a signal for distinguishing outcomes, and the analysis identifies conditions under which using that signal becomes increasingly advantageous.
icml-2025-scaling-test-time-compute-with.tldr: Under stated diversity and reward-distribution conditions, verification-guided training scales better than copying successful traces as test-time compute grows.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection depends heavily on the dataset, the application, and the detector’s settings. In a changing data stream, the best algorithm and hyperparameter combination can also change over time. SEAD addresses how to select among anomaly detectors when true anomaly labels are unavailable and future stream observations cannot be inspected in advance.

The proposed Streaming Ensemble of Anomaly Detectors performs unsupervised model selection as data arrive. It is designed to be computationally efficient, adaptable to non-stationary streams, and independent of the particular base detection algorithms being considered. These properties address a gap left by earlier selection methods that required supervision or access to the full test dataset offline.

Experiments on 14 public datasets and one internal dataset support the authors’ claims. The contribution is a selection mechanism for managing variation among detectors in a streaming setting. Its practical significance comes from combining adaptation with label-free operation: choosing a detector can respond to changing data without depending on a supply of confirmed anomalies.
icml-2025-sead-unsupervised-ensemble-of-.tldr: SEAD selects among streaming anomaly detectors without labeled anomalies and adapts as the data distribution changes.

paragraphs: People subject to a classifier may change their observable features to obtain a favorable decision. It can therefore seem attractive to hide the classifier and make manipulation harder. This paper formally studies whether restricting access improves the decision-maker’s performance when classifiers and strategic responses evolve over successive rounds.

The analysis changes a specific assumption of the standard model. Instead of knowing the current classifier and responding perfectly to it, agents act on a weighted average of previously implemented classifiers. Their behavior therefore depends on historical information. The model also represents possible feature changes with a manipulation graph, whose maximum in-degree measures how many distinct feature vectors can converge on one apparent vector.

In this setting, the authors derive mistake penalties of either 1/(1−γ) or the graph’s maximum in-degree relative to full classifier knowledge, with γ controlling memory of past classifiers. The result shows how withholding information can backfire under the modeled response behavior. Its implication is conditional on that historical-response setting: reduced transparency can increase classification errors rather than prevent them.
icml-2025-should-decision-makers-reveal-.tldr: Hiding the current classifier can increase mistakes when agents manipulate features using a weighted history of past classifiers.

paragraphs: Pruning compresses a neural network by removing weights judged to contribute little to performance. However, the resulting sparse model can differ substantially from the original dense one, especially when many weights are removed. This paper seeks to recover useful information lost through pruning by explicitly modeling the difference between dense and sparse weight matrices.

The method approximates that difference with a low-rank adjustment and iteratively refines the sparse matrix together with the correction. This provides a compact way to retain important information that individual weight-removal decisions may discard. The authors also analyze convergence, giving a theoretical foundation for the refinement procedure.

Experiments on LLaMa models demonstrate improvements across multiple pruning methods and sparsity levels. At 50% sparsity, the method reduces perplexity by 53.9% relative to conventional magnitude pruning on LLaMa-7B. For a specified performance target, it also enables an 8.6% parameter reduction while maintaining roughly 50% sparsity. These results show that targeted correction can improve the performance achievable with a pruned model.
icml-2025-targeted-low-rank-refinement-e.tldr: Iterative low-rank corrections recover information lost during language-model pruning and improve sparse-model performance.

paragraphs: Aligning time series means matching corresponding events even when they occur at different speeds or times. Dynamic Time Warping, or DTW, is a standard solution, but applying it to full signals can be slow and sensitive to noise. TimePoint learns a smaller representation on which DTW can operate more efficiently.

The method identifies informative keypoints and learns descriptors for them using self-supervision on synthetic data. To create training examples, it uses one-dimensional diffeomorphisms that model nonlinear changes in timing. Fully convolutional and wavelet convolutional architectures extract the keypoints and descriptors, adapting ideas from image keypoint detection to the different structure of one-dimensional signals.

DTW is then applied to these sparse representations instead of the complete signals. Despite training only on synthetic data, TimePoint generalizes well to real-world time series. The reported experiments show substantial speedups and improved alignment accuracy, while the broader claim is that accuracy typically improves. The result supports learning which signal locations are informative before carrying out the alignment.
icml-2025-timepoint-accelerated-time-ser.tldr: TimePoint learns sparse signal keypoints from synthetic data to accelerate DTW alignment and typically improve accuracy.

paragraphs: Explanations of model predictions can appear persuasive even when the analyst selected the model to obtain a preferred explanation. This paper calls that practice X-hacking. It studies how automated machine learning can search among models with similar predictive performance to find one whose explanation metrics, such as SHAP values, support a predetermined conclusion.

The authors formulate the search as a multi-objective optimization problem balancing accuracy and the desired explanation. This exploits model multiplicity: several defensible predictive models can yield different explanations. On the real-world datasets studied, Bayesian optimization accelerates X-hacking by an average factor of three compared with random sampling for features that are susceptible to it.

The study also links a dataset’s vulnerability to information redundancy among its features. This connects the opportunity for explanation manipulation to properties of the data itself. The authors suggest possible detection and prevention methods and discuss credibility and reproducibility. The central finding is that similar predictive accuracy can coexist with explanation differences that an automated search can deliberately exploit.
icml-2025-x-hacking-the-threat-of-misgui.tldr: Automated model search can exploit equally accurate models to produce preferred explanations, a practice the paper calls X-hacking.
